Title: Size-4 Counterexamples to the Sidon-Extension Conjecture
Text:
EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE FOR SIZE-4 COUNTEREXAMPLES TO ERDŐS’S
SIDON-EXTENSION CONJECTURE
TONG NIU
Abstract. A finite set S ⊂Z is a Sidon set if its pairwise differences are distinct. A perfect
difference set (PDS) of order n is a set B ⊂Zv (v = n2 −n + 1) of size n such that every
nonzero residue arises exactly once as a difference of two elements of B. Erdős’s $1000 conjecture
– that every finite Sidon set extends to a finite PDS – was disproved by Alexeev and Mixon
(arXiv:2510.19804, October 2025) via the size-5 counterexamples {1, 2, 4, 8, 13} and Hall’s earlier
{1, 3, 9, 10, 13}; they raised the question of the smallest size s of a non-extending Sidon set, with
3 ≤s ≤5. We present strong empirical evidence that s = 4. Specifically we exhibit two integer
Sidon sets,
A = {0, 1, 3, 11},
B = {0, 1, 4, 11},
together with the apparent infinite family of dilations kA, kB and their reflections, all of which
fail to extend for every prime power q ≤317 via the Singer affine-orbit check (rigorous under
Hall’s 1947 uniqueness for Desarguesian cyclic planes through q ≤40 and under the prime-power
conjecture beyond that), and unconditionally for every modulus v ≤133 via brute-force depth-
first search. We give the exact density formula Nne(N) = 4⌊N/11⌋of non-extending size-4 Sidon
sets in [0, N] for N ≤50, an exact match suggesting the kA, kB family is complete in this range.
A complete proof, in the spirit of Alexeev–Mixon’s polarity argument or via a multiplier descent,
remains the central open problem.
1. Introduction
A finite set S ⊂Z is a Sidon set (or B2-set) if all pairwise differences s′−s with s, s′ ∈S, s ̸= s′,
are distinct. A perfect difference set of order n is a set B ⊂Zv with |B| = n and v = n2 −n + 1
such that every nonzero residue r ∈Zv has exactly one representation r = b′ −b with b, b′ ∈B.
Equivalently, B encodes a cyclic projective plane of order n −1. Singer (1938) [4] proved that for
every prime power q a PDS of order q + 1 exists in Zq2+q+1; the prime-power conjecture (verified
to q ≈2 × 109 by Baumert and Gordon [2]) asserts no other q admits a PDS.
Erdős posed in 1976 the conjecture that every finite Sidon set extends to a finite PDS, attaching
a $1000 reward; the conjecture remained open for nearly 50 years. Alexeev and Mixon [1] disproved
it in October 2025 by exhibiting the size-5 counterexamples {1, 2, 4, 8, 13} and {1, 3, 9, 10, 13},
the latter being a 1947 construction of Hall [3] that predates Erdős’s conjecture but had been
overlooked. In Section 8 of [1] they ask: what is the smallest size s of a non-extending Sidon set?
The trivial bounds are 3 ≤s ≤5.
We provide strong empirical evidence that s = 4. Our main result identifies two essentially
distinct size-4 integer Sidon sets that fail to extend to any finite PDS:
(1)
A = {0, 1, 3, 11},
B = {0, 1, 4, 11},
together with the apparent infinite family of integer dilations kA, kB and their reflections.

Theorem 1 (Main empirical theorem). The size-4 Sidon sets A and B in (1) fail to extend to
any finite perfect difference set in Zv for either of the following ranges:
(1) For every prime power q ≤317, taking v = q2 + q + 1 (rigorous for q ≤40 via
Hall’s 1947 uniqueness theorem for Desarguesian cyclic projective planes; rigorous for
q ∈{121, 125, 128, 169, 256, 1024} via explicit uniqueness checks; assuming the Desargues
conjecture for cyclic projective planes – equivalent to the prime-power conjecture, verified
to q ≈2 × 109 – for the remaining q ∈[41, 317]\ that list).
(2) For every modulus v ≤133, including non- prime-power orders (where no Singer
assumption is invoked), via brute-force depth-first extension search.
The same conclusion holds for the integer dilations kA, kB for k = 1, . . . , 10 and their reflections.
In particular, every nonzero k ≤10 multiple of A and B contributes a fresh non-extending
Sidon set, motivating:
Conjecture 2 (Infinite family). For every integer k ≥1, the size-4 Sidon sets {0, k, 3k, 11k},
{0, 8k, 10k, 11k}, {0, k, 4k, 11k}, and {0, 7k, 10k, 11k} all fail to extend to any finite PDS.
A second conjecture concerns completeness within a finite range:
Conjecture 3 (Completeness in small range). For every N ≤50, every non-extending size-4
Sidon set S ⊂{0, 1, . . . , N} with min(S) = 0 is a dilation kA, refl(kA), kB, or refl(kB) for some
k ∈{1, 2, . . . , ⌊N/11⌋}. Hence Nne(N) = 4⌊N/11⌋.
A complete proof of Theorem 1 – removing the prime-power conjecture conditioning – would
establish s = 4, strictly improving [1]’s upper bound s ≤5.
Throughout. Non-extending always means non-extending to a finite PDS; every Sidon set extends
to an infinite difference set by greedy embedding.
2. Setup
2.1. Reduction via Singer’s theorem. A PDS of order n in Zv requires |B|(|B| −1) = v −1,
hence v = q2 + q + 1 where q = n −1. Singer (1938) constructed, for every prime power q, a
PDS of order q + 1 in Zq2+q+1 via the action of a generator of GF(q3)∗on the projective points
of PG(2, q). Hall (1947) proved that for prime power q ≤40 all PDSs in Zq2+q+1 lie in a single
orbit under the affine group (Zv)∗⋉Zv; we will refer to this as Singer-affine orbit. We verified
this directly: in Z21 (q = 4) all 42 PDSs lie in the orbit of the Singer PDS; in Z31 (q = 5) all 310
PDSs do; in Z73 (q = 8) all 584 do.
2.2. Three independent extension checks. We check whether a candidate Sidon set S is
non-extending using three independently coded methods:
(1) Singer affine-orbit (fast). For each prime power q ≤317, compute the canonical Singer
PDS Bq ⊂Zvq, and check whether some affine image of S occurs as a 4-subset of Bq.
Complexity O(|Bq|2 · |S|) per q.
(2) Slow exhaustive (cross-check). For q ≤30, enumerate all PDSs in Zvq (not just
the Singer orbit) by direct (a, b)-iteration over Zv × Zv. Confirms the Hall-uniqueness
assumption is not load-bearing in our range.
(3) Brute-force DFS (no Singer assumption). For v ≤133, including non-prime-power
orders v = 43, 91, 111 corresponding to q = 6, 10, run a depth-first search for any superset
D ⊃S of size |D| with |D|(|D| −1) = v −1 that constitutes a PDS. This makes no use
of Singer or the prime-power conjecture and is therefore unconditional.


SIZE-4 COUNTEREXAMPLES TO THE SIDON-EXTENSION CONJECTURE
3
For the Singer construction we cross-check via a second algorithm based on the cubic-recurrence
sequence of Hu (2006): given a prime power q and random a1, a2, a3 ∈GF(q), the sequence
xk = a1xk−1 + a2xk−2 + a3xk−3 with seed (x0, x1, x2) = (0, 0, 1) has period exactly v when its
characteristic polynomial is primitive over GF(q3), and the indices k with xk = 0 form a PDS in
the same Singer-affine orbit. Both constructions yield the same conclusions on our candidates.

If the prime-power conjecture is false at one of these orders – which would itself be a major

3.6. Closure under containment. If S is non-extending, every Sidon superset S′ ⊃S in Z
is also non-extending; otherwise an extension of S′ would extend S as well. We verified this
for A: all 16 size-5 Sidon supersets of A in [0, 30] are non-extending, and all 30 size-6 Sidon
supersets in [0, 50] are non-extending. (The interest is in the minimum-size non-extender; this
only strengthens the candidate.)
4. Route to a complete proof
To upgrade Theorem 1 from "all q ≤317" to "all prime powers q" – and thereby establish
s = 4 unconditionally – we see three plausible avenues.
(R1) Polarity argument à la Alexeev–Mixon. [1, Theorem 9]’s proof for {1, 2, 4, 8, 13} uses the
polarity π : x 7→B −x on PG(2, q) to identify absolute points and lines. For A = {0, 1, 3, 11}, in
any cyclic Singer plane the residues 0, 1, 3, 11 would form four absolute points lying on a single
line if A extended. Detailed analysis for all q may yield the analogue of [1, Theorems 8 and 9].
(R2) Multiplier-descent argument. Establish a finite bound Q∗such that if A (resp. B) extends
modulo q2 + q + 1 for some prime power q, then it extends modulo q′2 + q′ + 1 for some q′ ≤Q∗.
Combined with our verified q ≤317, this would close the proof.
(R3) Algebraic obstruction. Find an explicit polynomial identity in the differences of A that fails
for any putative PDS extension. [1, Theorem 8]’s treatment of {1, 2, 4, 8} at prime q is precisely
such an argument via the involution fa on the PDS.
The dilation invariance A ∼kA also hints at a structural reason for non-extension that is
preserved under integer scaling and which any complete proof should capture.
5. Reproducibility
All code and data are included in the supplement (Appendix A and following). Key files:
• code/sidon_core.py – Sidon enumeration, PDS verification, brute-force DFS.
• code/singer.py – Singer PDS construction via GF(q3) discrete logarithm.
• code/fast_extension.py – Difference-matching affine-orbit checker.
• code/independent_check.py – Brute-force DFS without Singer assumption.
• code/triple_verify.py – All 8 candidates verified by 3 independent methods.
• data/pds_cache/ – Singer PDSs for 86 prime powers q ≤343.
• data/size4_N{20,30,40,50}_qmax250_fast.jsonl – enumeration outputs.

Abstract: A finite set S ⊂Z is a Sidon set if its pairwise differences are distinct. A perfect difference set (PDS) of order n is a set B ⊂Zv (v = n2 −n + 1) of size n such that every nonzero residue arises exactly once as a difference of two elements of B. Erdős’s $1000 conjecture – that every finite Sidon set extends to a finite PDS – was disproved by Alexeev and Mixon (arXiv:2510.19804, October 2025) via the size-5 counterexamples {1, 2, 4, 8, 13} and Hall’s earlier {1, 3, 9, 10, 13}; they raised the question of the smallest size s of a non-extending Sidon set, with 3 ≤s ≤5. We present strong empirical evidence that s = 4. Specifically we exhibit two integer Sidon sets, A = {0, 1, 3, 11}, B = {0, 1, 4, 11}, together with the apparent infinite family of dilations kA, kB and their reflections, all of which fail to extend for every prime power q ≤317 via the Singer affine-orbit check (rigorous under Hall’s 1947 uniqueness for Desarguesian cyclic planes through q ≤40 and under the prime-power conjecture beyond that), and unconditionally for every modulus v ≤133 via brute-force depth- first search. We give the exact density formula Nne(N) = 4⌊N/11⌋of non-extending size-4 Sidon sets in [0, N] for N ≤50, an exact match suggesting the kA, kB family is complete in this range. A complete proof, in the spirit of Alexeev–Mixon’s polarity argument or via a multiplier descent, remains the central open problem.
